Is it true that for every $\epsilon,\eta>0$ there exists a $k$ such that the density of $n$ for which\[P(n(n+1)\cdots(n+k))>n^{1-\epsilon}\]is at least $1-\eta$ (where $P(m)$ is the greatest prime divisor of $m$)?

 On page 170 of [Er80], Erdos states he can only do this for $\epsilon = 1/2$.
But in this paper, in Theorem 1, he provides a proof for the problem with the bound of $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ and conjectures that it probably remains true if you replace $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ with $n^{1-\epsilon}$, which is the problem above.
This makes it sound like in [Er80], he made have made a mistake and meant he could prove this for the bound of $n^{1/2-\epsilon}$ and not $\epsilon=1/2$?

 Using known results for pair correlations between $P(n+i)$ and $P(n+j)$, e.g., from this paper of Teravainen, one should be able to prove a significantly stronger result, namely that for any $k$, one has $P(n \dots(n+k)) = n^{(\lambda + o_{k \to \infty}(1))k}$ on a set of logarithmic density $1 - o_{k \to \infty}(1)$, where $\lambda = 0.6243\dots$ is the Golomb-Dickman constant.
EDIT: Actually, this result doesn't quite strictly contain #1201 because it involves logarithmic density instead of natural density. On the other hand, it should be noted that Theorem 1.19 of Teravainen's paper already establishes $P(n (n+1)) > n^{2-\varepsilon}$ on a set of positive lower natural density.
SECOND EDIT: As pointed out below, the above comments actually apply to $P(n) \dots P(n+k)$ and $P(n) P(n+1)$ instead of $P(n \dots (n+k))$ and $P(n (n+1))$ respectively.

 Oops, you are right, thanks! So instead what Teravainen's results give is that $\asymp \varepsilon k$ of the $P(n),\dots,P(n+k)$ are of size at least $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for $n$ in a set of logarithmic density at least $1-\varepsilon$, but this is overkill for this problem.
(I was wondering why Erdos stated a result that seemed far weaker than what ought to be true, but it turns out that I misread the question, or more precisely I assumed incorrectly that $P$ was essentially multiplicative.)
On the other hand, #1201 remains technically open because it was not established that the natural density of the set $\{ n: P(n \dots (n+k)) \geq n^{1-\varepsilon}\}$ actually exists; instead, it is shown that the natural lower density is at least $1-\eta$.

 \#\{n\le N:P ^{+}((n)\cdots(n+h-1))\le n^\alpha\}
